  B.  Appropriation of Funds in the Amount of $460,000 from the Office of Traffic
  Safety Grant (Reimbursement Grant)

  Recommended Action: Provide a recommendation to the City Council concerning
  the appropriation of funds in the amount of $460,000 from the Office of Traffic
  Safety Grant (Reimbursement Grant).

  Deputy City Manager Brown discussed the Office of Traffic Safety (OTS)
  reimbursement grant. She stated that under the grant, enforcement operations would
  be in collaboration with law enforcement agencies. She stated the City would
  facilitate four DUI checkpoints, one per quarter, and eight general enforcement
  saturation operations, two per quarter. She stated the general enforcement
  operations were based on traffic accident primary collision factors, which included
  failure to yield to pedestrians, distracted driving, and reckless driving. She provided
  highlights of the public educational campaign, which included a 21 Miles on
  Malibu experiential event. She stated that educational programs needed to be
  approved by the City Council.

  In response to City Manager McClary, Deputy City Manager Brown stated that any
  funding attached to the grant needed to be expended during the 2024/2025 federal
  fiscal year, October 1, 2024 through September 30, 2025. She stated that if an
  unforeseen circumstance arose, the funding would at least need to be obligated
  during the 2024/2025 federal fiscal year.

  In response to Councilmember Silverstein, Deputy City Manager Brown stated that
  a contract could be signed and paid during the fiscal year and then services
  scheduled for a later time, but services needed to be provided prior to the end of the
  federal fiscal year. She stated that the City would pay for the checkpoints that would
  be scheduled and staffed by the Los Angeles County Sheriff Department. She stated
  that the Sheriff Department would provide a report and invoice to the City and the
  City would submit the request for reimbursement to the OTS against the grant funds
  before the end of the federal fiscal year. She stated that the Sheriff Department
  would not have to wait for payment by the City until the City received the
  reimbursed grant funds.

  City Manager McClary added that he did not anticipate difficulties in using the
  funds and applying for reimbursement during the time allowed.

  Mayor Stewart stated that the grant funds are federal funds sent to the States which
  are then distributed to the City.

  In response to Mayor Stewart, Deputy City Manager Brown stated that the scope
  of work proposed was informed by input from law enforcement agencies. She stated
  the amount going toward education was what was recommended by the OTS. She
  stated that the remaining funds of $44,040 were proposed to be used toward
  enforcement if staffing could be arranged. She stated the grant funds could not be

  used toward California Highway Patrol (CHP) staffing, as they were a State agency.
  She stated neighboring City police departments could provide services under the
  grant. She stated there could be opportunities for collaboration with other law
  enforcement agencies utilizing other funding.

  In response to Mayor Stewart and Councilmember Silverstein, Deputy City
  Manager Brown stated that enforcement was a priority, and it was determined that
  the four DUI checkpoints and eight saturation operations could be facilitated by the
  City, and $325,000 was recommended to go toward education by the OTS.

  In response to Councilmember Silverstein, Deputy City Manager Brown stated that
  racing was not identified as a primary collision factor by OTS for this grant. She
  stated that racing was a significant issue in Malibu, and the City was exploring
  enforcement in the canyons and on Pacific Coast Highway (PCH). She stated that
  checkpoints and saturation operations were not announced beforehand.

  Mayor Stewart added that enforcement of racing noise involved specialized training
  and equipment.

  City Manager McClary stated that what was found to be effective in changing
  people’s behavior to follow City rules was to schedule days canvassing problematic
  areas, with enforcement issuing a warning the first time, and in the following days
  everyone cited who were not in compliance with the rules. He stated that word
  would spread, and people were less likely to break the rules and risk a citation. He
  suggested a similar approach for racing noise.

  Deputy City Manager Brown added that much of the noise was caused by illegal
  modification of vehicles.

  Councilmember Silverstein added that motorcycles also contributed to noise in the
  canyons.

  Mayor Stewart discussed timing. He stated that his wife observed two CHP cars
  and two Sheriff Department cars issuing citations on PCH on a Thursday morning.
  He stated that much of the speeding occurred on the weekends and Wednesday,
  Thursday, and Friday nights. He stated that the most coveted shifts for enforcement
  staff were daytime, Monday through Friday and inquired how enforcement staffing
  might be provided during more effective times.

  In response to Mayor Stewart, Deputy City Manager Brown stated operations
  specific to this grant would be conducted at peak times to have the most impact.
  She stated that they wanted the word to get out that there was an increased
  enforcement presence. She stated that information on peak times was available
  from the Sheriff's Office and that peak DUI times were between Thursday and
  Saturday nights and holidays.

  Mayor Stewart discussed from his marketing experience the importance of having
  measurable results and that 21 Miles in Malibu had an acknowledged result. He
  discussed a breakdown of costs and measurement of benefits and results. He stated
  that level one marketing was brand identification.

  In response to Mayor Stewart, Deputy City Manager Brown stated that Malibu was
  its own brand, and the Cruise Malibu campaign was rebranded as Malibu Surf,
  Sand, Slow and was directed towards residents and visitors. She stated the City
  sought allocation of $325,000 toward the educational campaign and a more
  identified marketing plan was forthcoming. She stated it would be a comprehensive,
  all-encompassing strategy, including the 21 Miles in Malibu experiential event
  which was directed toward young students and would serve as a model for other
  communities. She stated media metrics would be tracked and reported and that
  participants would be polled for an evaluation of program effectiveness. She stated
  that City staff was working with Michel Shane and Malibu High School PTSA on
  development of the program. She stated that Every 15 Minutes program was not
  sustainable due to the high costs of holding the two-day event.

  In response to Councilmember Silverstein, Deputy City Manager Brown stated that
  other community stakeholders included the PTSA and school district. She
  discussed the Los Angeles County PCH Safety Week.

  Mayor Stewart stated that the 21 Miles in Malibu program was much more cost
  effective than the Red Asphalt and Every 15 Minutes programs. He discussed how
  Pepperdine University and surrounding communities contributed to traffic safety
  issues.

  In response to Mayor Stewart, Deputy City Manager Brown stated that they wanted
  a Malibu first approach which could then be replicated outside of the City. She
  stated a Pepperdine focus group was established and had good participation. She
  stated that students wanted to be involved in PCH safety and other educational
  initiatives which included the Chamber of Commerce and local realtors. She stated
  that everyone had the same intention of making PCH and Malibu safer.

  Councilmember Silverstein stated that the danger of unsafe behavior on PCH
  should be the main message. He stated that the Cruise Malibu campaign
  emphasized the appeal of Malibu and encouraged visitors to drive safely but did
  not convey the dangers. He stated that the campaign should not emphasize the
  attractiveness of Malibu; they needed to ensure visitors were safe.

  Deputy City Manager Brown stated that she understood how the Cruise Malibu
  campaign was perceived, but the intent was to educate visitors on behaving safely
  and encouraging drivers to set their cruise control at or below the speed limit.

  Commissioner Silverstein stated that he would like to see more of the repercussions
  of people not conducting themselves safely and responsibly.

  Deputy City Manager Brown stated that messaging needed to reach people while
  providing statistics and the realities of unsafe behavior.

  Commissioner Silverstein stated that residents see a car flipped over on the highway
  very frequently.

  Deputy City Manager Brown stated that many individuals followed celebrities on
  social media and having them involved broadened the audience. She stated that
  having a broad strategy helped the message reach all the different target audiences.
  She stated that the City Council needed to decide what level the City wanted to
  control the messaging.

  Councilmember Silverstein stated that he received a campaign contribution from
  Colin Drummond, and if Mr. Drummond was involved, he might need to recuse
  himself.

  In response to Councilmember Silverstein, Deputy City Manager Brown stated that
  she would check with the City Attorney if Councilmember Silverstein would need
  to recuse himself if something was brought before the City Council, but the current
  discussion was allocation of funds.

  Commissioner Silverstein stated that he wanted confirmation, and other
  Councilmembers might need to recuse themselves.

  Mayor Stewart stated that his understanding was that there was a State law passed
  recently that contributions of $250 or greater were cause for recusal.

  Mayor Stewart stated that it appeared the action requested was a recommendation
  for the appropriation of funds toward enforcement as discussed and public relations,
  with details, metrics, and an expenditure plan forthcoming.

  Councilmember Silverstein stated that he wanted to ensure that he was not doing
  something wrong by supporting the recommendation, in terms of the financial
  issue.

  City Manager McClary stated that he thought Councilmember Silverstein would
  not need to recuse himself at this point because an approval for a contract or
  agreement was not being sought.

  Councilmember Silverstein stated that if he was not doing anything wrong, then he
  supported the recommendation.

  City Manager McClary stated that he was happy to go on the record that nothing
  was improper, but he understood his concerns.

  Mayor Stewart stated that he appreciated Councilmember Silverstein’s diligence
  on the matter.

MOTION  Mayor Stewart moved, and Councilmember Silverstein seconded a motion to
  recommend to the City Council approval of the appropriation of funds in the
  amount of $460,000 from the Office of Traffic Safety Grant (Reimbursement
  Grant). The motion carried unanimously.

Subject:  Fund Balance Policy of the General Fund – Council Policy #3

RECOMMENDED ACTION: Provide direction to staff regarding Council Policy #3 – Fund
Balance Policy.

FISCAL IMPACT: There is no fiscal impact associated with the recommended action. As
of June 24, 2024, the projected General Fund Undesignated Reserve at June 30, 2025, is
$69.45 million.

WORK PLAN:  This item is included in the FY 2024-25 Proposed Strategic Priority Plan
supporting Fund Balance Policy priority.

DISCUSSION: The City of Malibu is fortunate to be in a strong financial position with
healthy reserve balances. At the time of the adoption of the FY 2024-25 Budget, the
General Fund Undesignated1 Reserve has a projected ending balance of $69.45 million
at June 30, 2025. The projected ending balance is 115.3% of the FY 2024-25 General
Fund Program Expenditures of $60.23 million. This exceeds the City’s goal of maintaining
a minimum of 50% of the budgeted expenditures in reserves (Council Policy #3) and
exceeds the 65% goal necessary to retain the highest credit rating for the City (per the
City’s underwriter). In addition, there is $6.5 million in Fund Balance designated for
contingencies. The total projected General Fund balance (including Designated and
Undesignated Reserves) at June 30, 2025, is $83.04 million. These reserves are detailed
on the Schedule of Fund Balances page of the budget.

1
 Governmental Accounting Standards Board (GASB) Statement No. 54, defines fund balance terms. Undesignated should be
Unassigned per GASB 54. For the purposes of this report, Undesignated and Unassigned will be used interchangeably.

  Agenda Item 3.B.
  Page 10 of 16
 Existing City Council Policy #3 (see attachment), adopted in 1997, establishes that the
General Fund Undesignated Reserve maintains a minimum amount of General Fund of at
least fifty (50) percent of budgeted fiscal year expenditures for its General Fund. Due to
the strength of the City’s reserves, the City Council requested a review of the policy for
potential modifications to further delineate fund balance designations.

In comparing the City of Malibu Fund Balance Policy to other similar agencies, Malibu’s is
on the conservative end, putting the City on very stable footing. Maintaining this
conservative financial posture is advised. The breakdown of benchmark cities is as
follows:

City  Policy  Notes
Malibu  50.0%
Agoura Hills  40.0%
Beverly Hills  40.0%  25% contingency; 15% short-term community economic
  investment; additional Budget Stabilization Reserve
Calabasas  10.0%
Camarillo  50.0%
Culver City  30.0%  Contingency reserve (30%), surpluses place 10% in Public
  Safety Equipment <$1M, remainder to Unassigned
Laguna Beach  20.0%  10% per municipal code, but Council policy 20%
Manhattan Beach 20.0%
Redondo Beach  8.33%
Thousand Oaks  20.0%  5% emergency contingency for economic uncertainties;
  15% Working Capital Reserve
West Hollywood  35.0%

The Government Finance Officers Association (GFOA) recommends, “at a minimum, that
general-purpose governments, regardless of size, maintain unrestricted budgetary fund
balance in their general fund of no less than two months of regular general fund operating
revenues or regular general fund operating expenditures.” A two month fund balance is
about 17% of operating expenditures. Furthermore, Unrestricted Funds are considered a
combination of Committed, Assigned, and Unassigned Fund Balances as outlined below.

  Agenda Item 3.B.
  Page 11 of 16
 Governmental Accounting Standards Board (GASB) Statement 54:
In adhering to GAAP, the City follows GASB 54, which addresses Fund Balance Reporting
and defines the terms, in the City’s Annual Comprehensive Financial Report (ACFR).
Compliance in the governmental fund financial statements requires that fund balance be
made up of the categories below. The City’s Budget is currently using the terms
Undesignated and Designated, but staff will work on aligning the budget terms with the
ACFR and GASB terms. The GASB 54 Fund Balance terms are outlined in the ACFR as
follows:

Restricted:
  • Nonspendable fund balance typically includes inventories, prepaid items, and other
  similar items that must be maintained intact pursuant to legal or contractual
  requirements.

  • Restricted fund balance includes amounts that can be spent only for specific
  purposes imposed by creditors, grantors, contributors, or laws or regulations of
  other governments or through enabling legislation.

Unrestricted:
  • Committed fund balance includes amounts that can be used only for the specific
  purposes determined by a resolution (formal action) of the City Council. The City
  Council has the authority to establish, modify, or rescind a fund balance
  commitment.

  • Assigned fund balance is comprised of amounts designated by the City Council for
  specific purposes that do not meet the criteria to be classified as restricted or
  committed. In accordance with the City’s fund balance policy, the City Council may
  assign a designee, the City Manager, to make assignments of fund balance.

  • Unassigned fund balance is the residual classification that includes all spendable
  amounts not contained in other categories. The General Fund is the only fund that
  may report a positive unassigned fund balance. In all other governmental funds,
  when expenditures exceed the amounts available, it may be necessary to report a
  negative unassigned fund balance in that fund.

When expenditures are incurred for purposes for which both restricted and unrestricted
(committed, assigned, or unassigned) fund balances are available, the City’s policy is to
consider restricted fund balance to have been depleted before using any components of
unrestricted fund balance. Further, when expenditures are incurred for purposes for which
committed, assigned, or unassigned fund balances are available, the City’s policy is to first
deplete committed fund balance, then assigned fund balance, and finally unassigned fund
balance.

  Agenda Item 3.B.
  Page 12 of 16
 Policy Recommendation:
Maintaining a conservative budget posture is a sound fiscal practice. The existing policy
requires a 50% Unassigned reserve and shall remain in-place. Staff suggest that Council
maintain Council Policy #3 as is and consider whether to Commit additional surplus funds
to specific uses through formal action, typically done as part of the budget adoption
process or as part of fiscal year reporting. Maintaining an Unassigned Fund Balance
beyond the 50% policy requirement provides the Council with the broadest flexibility to
appropriate the funds for strategic purposes.

As an example, the FY 2024-25 Adopted Budget projected a Year-End Fund Balance of
$69.45 million on June 30, 2025. The FY 2024-25 General Fund expenditures are adopted
at $60.23 million. A 50% minimum reserve would be $30.12 million, leaving about $39.33
million Unassigned for strategic purposes.

  FY 2024-25
  GF Expenditures  $ 60,230,000
  Policy #3  50%
  Min Reserve  30,120,000
  YE Projected Unassigned FB  69,450,000
  Unassigned Surplus  $ 39,330,000

The Council could choose to deliberate on the remaining $39.33 million balance to Commit
funds as part of the budget adoption process, or during the current FY 2024-25 Mid-Year,
or a workshop could be scheduled. Lastly, as an option, the Unassigned Fund Balance
can be left as is and the funds can be Committed when necessary.

Subject:  Funding For Dial-A-Ride Transportation Services

RECOMMENDED ACTION: Provide a recommendation to the City Council on the
appropriation of $144,000 from Prop A funding for Dial-A-Ride Transportation Services.

FISCAL IMPACT: Dial-A-Ride Transportation was included in the Adopted Budget for
FY 2024-25 in the amount of $127,500 in Account No. 203-3009-5145-00 (Proposition
A Transportation Services - Dial-A-Ride Services). An appropriation of $144,000 from
Prop A funding is required for a new service contract. The additional appropriation
would bring the amended FY 2024-25 budget to $271,500. The unaudited Prop A Fund
Balance on June 30, 2024, is $647,789.

WORK PLAN: This item is part of the day-to-day operations identified in the Adopted
FY 2024-25 Strategic Priority Project List.

DISCUSSION: Council Policy #44 requires that all proposed appropriations over
$10,000 be reviewed and discussed by the Administration and Finance Subcommittee
prior to being presented to the City Council. The proposed appropriation item will be
presented to the Council at its Regular meeting on November 12, 2024.

The City’s Dial-A-Ride (DAR) Program provides low-cost transportation services to
senior residents (ages 60 and older) and for residents of any age who are disabled from
operating a motor vehicle as defined by the California Vehicle Code.

  Agenda Item 3.C.
  Page 15 of 16
 Riders pay $1.00 each way for trips to the Malibu Senior Center, $2.00 each way for
trips within City limits, and $4.00 each way for trips outside of City limits. DAR program
boundaries include the following:

  •  City of Malibu, City Limits
  •  City of Agoura Hills, City Limits
  •  City of Calabasas (North of Las Virgenes Canyon Road)
  •  City of Santa Monica between California Avenue and Colorado Avenue and
  •  Kaiser Permanente in Woodland Hills
  •  UCLA Medical Center in West Los Angeles
  •  Veterans’ Medical Center in West Los Angeles

A Request for Proposal (RFP) was released in July 2024, with the City receiving two
proposals by the September 6, 2024 deadline. Staff reviewed the proposals,
interviewed the transportation agencies, and selected RTW Management, Inc. (RTW).
RTW has experience providing services for various municipalities, excellent references,
and the ability to provide residents with services that meet their transportation needs.
RTW will utilize new ADA-compliant accessible hybrid vehicles compliant with the
Federal Transit Administration. Vehicles will have a digital radio system for dispatchers
to communicate with drivers. The customer call center will use advanced scheduling
and dispatching systems to optimize routes and real-time tracing technology to monitor
vehicle location, speed, and route.

As part of the Agreement and the costs associated with providing services, RTW will
provide all the fleet, fuel, maintenance, drivers, training, insurance, personnel for the
call center and dispatch, telephone lines, and transportation software systems.

The City uses Prop A funds to cover the costs associated with the DAR program. The
City receives approximately $295,000 annually and has a balance fund of
approximately $647,000. The excess funds may be used to supplement the annual
DAR costs, but general fund money will likely be needed after 3 years to continue the
DAR program at the current level. Staff are also investigating options for grant funding
to supplement the transportation service costs.
